title: Classification of offences and the first hearing
subtitle: Summary, either-way and indictable-only offences, and plea before venue
objectives: Distinguish summary-only, either-way and indictable-only offences, and give an example of each
Explain why every adult defendant's first appearance takes place in the magistrates' court regardless of the offence's seriousness
Apply the plea before venue procedure to a given either-way case, including the consequences of an indicated guilty plea

leadingAuthorities.role: Governs the plea before venue procedure for either-way offences

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often conflate 'serious offence' with 'starts in the Crown Court'. Where the profile shows this confusion, this brief note appears: 'Every case starts in the same place — what changes is what happens next.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can define the three categories. The test pool here leans on scenarios that ask what happens procedurally, not just what an offence is called — focus on the sequence of steps.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Parts 1 and 2 and fix the three offence categories and their examples before moving on — the plea before venue procedure in Part 3 assumes you already know which offences it applies to.

overview.hook: A defendant charged with murder and a defendant charged with speeding both walk into the same building on their first morning in the criminal justice system: the magistrates' court. One of them will never see the inside of a Crown Court; the other's case may barely touch the magistrates' court at all. This lesson is about how the system decides, in the space of one hearing, which is which.

parts.heading: Three categories, one starting gate
parts.voice: structural — sets out the map before the detail
body: Every criminal offence in England and Wales falls into one of three categories, and the category determines which court (or courts) can ultimately try it. Summary-only offences can only be tried in the magistrates' court — common examples include most road traffic offences and common assault. Indictable-only offences are the most serious and can only be tried in the Crown Court, before a judge and jury — murder, manslaughter and robbery are classic examples. Either-way offences sit in between and can be tried in either court, depending on the outcome of the procedure covered later in this lesson — theft and assault occasioning actual bodily harm are typical examples.

It is tempting to assume that offence seriousness maps neatly onto which court a case starts in. It doesn't. Every adult defendant, whatever they are charged with, makes their first appearance in the magistrates' court. That is true for a shoplifter and a murder suspect alike — the magistrates' court is the single point of entry for the entire system.

What differs is what happens at, and after, that first hearing. An indictable-only case is sent almost immediately to the Crown Court (a mechanism covered in the next lesson). A summary-only case stays in the magistrates' court throughout. An either-way case goes through its own dedicated procedure — plea before venue — to work out where it belongs.

components.label: The three offence categories
points: Summary-only — tried only in the magistrates' court (e.g. most driving offences, common assault)
Either-way — tried in either court, depending on plea before venue and allocation (e.g. theft, ABH)
Indictable-only — tried only in the Crown Court (e.g. murder, manslaughter, robbery)

interaction.prompt: A defendant is charged with common assault. In which court, or courts, can this offence be tried?
options: Magistrates' court only
Crown Court only
Either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court
Neither — it is dealt with entirely outside the court system
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Common assault is a summary-only offence — it can never be sent to the Crown Court for trial.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Common assault is summary-only, meaning the magistrates' court is the only court with jurisdiction to try it — unlike an either-way offence, there is no route to Crown Court trial here.

parts.heading: Why the first hearing is always the same
parts.voice: argumentative — explains the logic behind a counterintuitive rule
body: It can feel strange that a murder suspect first appears in the same building, before the same tier of court, as someone accused of a parking offence. The reason is administrative and protective rather than about seriousness: the magistrates' court is the system's single point of entry because it is where basic, urgent matters are dealt with quickly — confirming identity, dealing with bail or remand, and, for indictable-only offences, sending the case onward without delay.

For an indictable-only offence, the magistrates' court's role at this stage is deliberately minimal: it has no power to try the case, and its job is essentially administrative — confirm the charge, deal with bail, and send the case to the Crown Court (the mechanism examined in Lesson 9). The magistrates are not assessing guilt, evidence, or venue in any substantive sense at this point.

For summary-only and either-way offences, by contrast, the first hearing in the magistrates' court is doing real work: entering pleas, and — for either-way offences — beginning the plea before venue procedure that determines where the case will ultimately be dealt with.

components.term: Magistrates' court as point of entry
components.definition: Every adult defendant's first court appearance is in the magistrates' court, regardless of the offence charged. For indictable-only offences this hearing is largely administrative; for summary and either-way offences it is where plea and (for either-way offences) venue are determined.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you this defendant's first hearing will be purely administrative rather than involve a plea before venue procedure.
interaction.scenarioText: An adult defendant is charged with robbery, an indictable-only offence, and makes his first appearance before the magistrates' court the following morning.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — because the offence is indictable-only, the magistrates' court has no trial jurisdiction over it at all, so the first hearing is confined to administrative matters like bail before the case is sent to the Crown Court.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The key fact is the offence's classification, not the defendant's age or the fact of a first appearance — every defendant has a first appearance, but only an indictable-only classification removes any question of plea before venue.

parts.heading: Plea before venue: what s 17A actually requires
parts.voice: structural — works through the statutory procedure step by step
body: For an either-way offence, the first hearing follows a specific statutory procedure known as plea before venue, set out in s 17A of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980. The charge is read to the defendant (or, in practice, its substance explained), and the defendant is asked to indicate how they would plead if the matter were to proceed to trial.

The defendant has three possible responses: an indication of a guilty plea, an indication of a not guilty plea, or no indication at all (silence is treated as an indication of a not guilty plea for these purposes). What happens next depends entirely on which of these is given.

The plea before venue stage exists to avoid wasting the more resource-intensive allocation procedure (covered in the next lesson) on cases where the defendant is going to plead guilty anyway — there is no need to ask which court is better suited to a contested trial that will never happen.

components.text: Where a person who has attained the age of 18 years appears or is brought before a magistrates' court on an information charging him with an offence triable either way... the court shall explain to him... that he may indicate whether (if the offence were to proceed to trial) he would plead guilty or not guilty, and that if he indicates that he would plead guilty the court must proceed as if the proceedings were the summary trial of the information.
elements: Defendant invited to indicate a plea
Guilty indication treated as summary trial from that point
Not guilty indication (or no indication) moves to allocation

interaction.prompt: Under s 17A of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, what is the defendant asked to do at the plea before venue stage?
options: Formally enter a binding plea that cannot later be changed under any circumstances
Indicate how they would plead if the case proceeded to trial
Elect immediately whether they want a jury trial, before any indication of plea
Choose their own sentence range in advance of any finding of guilt
interaction.explanation: Section 17A asks for an indication of plea, not a final binding plea and not an election of court — the indication is what determines the next procedural step.

parts.heading: Following an indicated guilty plea
parts.voice: direct — traces the consequence through to its end point
body: If the defendant indicates a guilty plea, the consequence is immediate and significant: the case proceeds as if it were a summary trial, meaning the magistrates deal with it themselves. There is no allocation procedure and no question of Crown Court trial — the plea before venue stage has, in effect, resolved the venue question by removing the need to choose one.

The magistrates then either sentence the defendant themselves or, if they consider their sentencing powers are insufficient for the offence, commit the case to the Crown Court for sentence only (the trial having already effectively concluded by virtue of the guilty plea). This is a narrower step than sending a case for trial — it is purely about sentencing power, not venue for a contested hearing.
This sequencing rewards an early guilty plea with certainty and, in practice, with sentencing credit — a theme that recurs throughout SQE1 criminal practice.

components.title: Plea before venue — what follows each response
components.description: The procedural consequence of each possible response to the plea before venue question.

nodes.label: Defendant indicates plea to an either-way offence
Guilty indicated — proceed as summary trial
Magistrates sentence, or commit for sentence only if powers insufficient
Not guilty indicated (or no indication) — move to allocation procedure

components.textAlternative: If the defendant indicates a guilty plea, the case proceeds as a summary trial and the magistrates either sentence the defendant or commit for sentence only if their powers are insufficient. If the defendant indicates a not guilty plea, or gives no indication, the case moves instead to the allocation procedure.

interaction.prompt: Order these steps following an indicated guilty plea to an either-way offence.
items: Charge explained; defendant indicates a guilty plea
Case proceeds as if it were a summary trial
Magistrates assess whether their sentencing powers are sufficient
Magistrates sentence, or commit to the Crown Court for sentence only
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence — an indicated guilty plea converts the case into a summary trial outcome immediately, leaving only the sentencing-power question open.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — the case becomes a summary trial as soon as the guilty plea is indicated; the question of committal is only about sentencing power, and comes after that conversion, not before it.

parts.heading: Following an indicated not guilty plea
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the contrast before resolving it
body: What if the defendant indicates a not guilty plea instead — or says nothing at all? Here the case cannot simply proceed as a summary trial, because there has been no acceptance of guilt to convert the matter into one. Instead, the case moves on to the allocation procedure, examined fully in the next lesson, which decides whether the case is suitable for summary trial or should go to the Crown Court.

No indication at all is treated, for these purposes, as equivalent to an indication of not guilty — a defendant cannot avoid the allocation procedure simply by refusing to answer. This detail is easy to miss and is a favourite exam trap: silence is not neutral, it defaults to not guilty for plea before venue purposes.

The contrast to hold onto: an indicated guilty plea short-circuits the venue question entirely (the case simply becomes a summary matter); an indicated not guilty plea (or no indication) hands the venue question over to the allocation procedure, where both the court and, in some circumstances, the defendant have a say.

components.definition: Under the plea before venue procedure, a defendant who gives no indication of plea is treated as if they had indicated a not guilty plea, and the case proceeds to the allocation procedure exactly as it would on an express not guilty indication.

interaction.prompt: Two defendants, both charged with theft (an either-way offence). Which one moves to the allocation procedure?
interaction.scenarioA: Defendant A is asked to indicate a plea and clearly states she would plead guilty.
interaction.scenarioB: Defendant B is asked to indicate a plea and declines to say anything at all.
interaction.explanation: A's guilty indication converts the case into a summary trial with no need for allocation. B's silence is treated as a not guilty indication, so B's case proceeds to allocation — silence does not avoid the procedure.

testPool.prompt: Which category of offence can only be tried in the Crown Court?
options: Summary-only
Either-way
Indictable-only
Hybrid
testPool.explanation: Indictable-only offences, such as murder and robbery, can only be tried in the Crown Court before a judge and jury.

testPool.prompt: In which court does every adult defendant make their first appearance, whatever offence they are charged with?
options: The Crown Court
The magistrates' court
The relevant appellate court
Whichever court the defendant elects
testPool.explanation: The magistrates' court is the universal point of entry for adult criminal proceedings, regardless of the offence's classification or seriousness.

testPool.prompt: What is the purpose of the plea before venue procedure under s 17A of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980?
options: To determine whether a summary-only offence should instead be treated as indictable
To invite an either-way offence defendant to indicate a plea before the question of trial venue is addressed
To decide whether an indictable-only offence should be downgraded to either-way
To fix the defendant's sentence in advance of any trial
testPool.explanation: Plea before venue applies specifically to either-way offences and asks for an indication of plea before, and in order to inform, any question of venue.

testPool.prompt: A defendant charged with an either-way offence says nothing when asked to indicate a plea. How is this treated under the plea before venue procedure?
options: As an indication of a guilty plea
As an indication of a not guilty plea
As an automatic acquittal
As grounds to adjourn indefinitely with no further procedure
testPool.explanation: Silence is treated as equivalent to an indicated not guilty plea, so the case proceeds to the allocation procedure exactly as it would on an express not guilty indication.

testPool.prompt: Why does the magistrates' court's role at the first hearing for an indictable-only offence not involve plea before venue?
options: Because indictable-only offences never have a first hearing at all
Because the magistrates' court has no jurisdiction to try indictable-only offences, so its role is limited to administrative matters before sending the case to the Crown Court
Because plea before venue only applies to offences carrying a custodial sentence
Because indictable-only defendants are entitled to skip the magistrates' court entirely
testPool.explanation: Plea before venue exists to resolve venue for either-way offences. Indictable-only offences have only one possible venue — the Crown Court — so there is nothing for the procedure to resolve.

testPool.prompt: A defendant is charged with theft, then indicates she would plead guilty when asked under the plea before venue procedure. What happens next?
options: The case is automatically sent to the Crown Court for trial, since theft is a serious offence
The case proceeds as if it were a summary trial, with the magistrates dealing with it or committing for sentence only if their powers are insufficient
The magistrates must still carry out an allocation hearing before proceeding further
The indicated guilty plea has no procedural effect until the trial date is fixed
testPool.trapExplanation: Candidates sometimes assume seriousness (or the fact that theft is either-way) means the case automatically goes to Crown Court. An indicated guilty plea converts the case into a summary matter regardless of seriousness — allocation is never reached.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following statements about offence classification is correct?
options: Summary-only offences can be sent to the Crown Court if the magistrates consider them serious enough
Either-way offences are tried summarily or on indictment depending on the outcome of plea before venue and, where relevant, allocation — not on seriousness alone
Indictable-only offences can be tried summarily if the defendant consents
All offences are either-way unless a statute expressly says otherwise
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to think summary-only offences can somehow escalate, or that indictable-only offences can be downgraded by consent — neither is true. Only either-way offences have a genuine choice of venue, decided through the statutory procedure, not simply by how serious the facts appear.

testPool.prompt: A defendant charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm (an either-way offence) indicates a not guilty plea at the plea before venue hearing. What is the correct next procedural step?
options: The magistrates proceed immediately to a summary trial without any further procedure
The case moves to the allocation procedure to determine the appropriate venue
The case is automatically committed to the Crown Court for trial without further steps
The charge is dismissed because a not guilty plea has been entered
testPool.trapExplanation: A not guilty indication does not mean an automatic Crown Court trial, nor does it mean an immediate summary trial — it triggers the allocation procedure, which is the mechanism that actually decides venue.

testPool.prompt: A defendant is charged with driving with excess alcohol, a summary-only offence. Which of the following correctly describes the venue for trial?
options: It can only be tried in the magistrates' court
It can be tried in either the magistrates' court or the Crown Court, depending on plea before venue
It can only be tried in the Crown Court given the road safety implications
The defendant may elect Crown Court trial if she wishes
testPool.explanation: Summary-only offences have no route to the Crown Court at all — plea before venue and allocation are procedures that apply only to either-way offences.

testPool.prompt: A defendant charged with fraud (an either-way offence) indicates a guilty plea, and the magistrates conclude their sentencing powers are insufficient for the seriousness of the offending. What should happen?
options: The magistrates must acquit and refer the matter for a fresh charge
The magistrates proceed as if it were a summary trial, but commit the defendant to the Crown Court for sentence only
The case restarts from the beginning of the plea before venue procedure
The magistrates ignore the sentencing limitation and pass an unlawful sentence
testPool.explanation: An indicated guilty plea already converts the matter into a summary trial outcome; where the magistrates' sentencing powers are insufficient, the correct route is committal for sentence only, not a fresh trial process.

testPool.prompt: A defendant is charged with murder. Which of the following correctly describes the role of the magistrates' court at the first hearing?
options: The magistrates conduct plea before venue in the usual way
The magistrates carry out the allocation procedure to decide venue
The magistrates' role is essentially administrative — dealing with matters such as bail before sending the case to the Crown Court
The magistrates try the case themselves given its seriousness
testPool.explanation: Murder is indictable-only, so there is no venue question to resolve and no plea before venue or allocation procedure — the magistrates' court's role is confined to administrative matters.

testPool.prompt: Under s 17A of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, which offences trigger the plea before venue procedure?
options: Summary-only offences
Either-way offences
Indictable-only offences
All criminal offences without distinction
testPool.explanation: Section 17A is specifically directed at either-way offences — offences that could, depending on plea and allocation, be tried either summarily or on indictment.

testPool.prompt: Section 17A provides that if the defendant indicates a guilty plea, the court must proceed as if the case were 'the summary trial of the information'. What is the practical effect of this wording?
options: It has no practical effect; the allocation procedure still applies in full
It converts the case procedurally into a summary matter, removing the need for allocation to decide venue
It requires the case to be sent to the Crown Court regardless of the plea
It means the defendant must be formally tried even though they have indicated guilt
testPool.explanation: This is the operative effect of an indicated guilty plea: the venue question is resolved automatically because the case is treated as summary from that point, with allocation never engaged.

testPool.prompt: A defendant charged with an either-way offence gives no indication of plea when invited to do so under s 17A. Applying the statutory procedure, what is the correct next step?
options: Treat the silence as an indicated guilty plea and proceed to sentencing
Treat the silence as an indicated not guilty plea and move to the allocation procedure
Adjourn indefinitely until the defendant responds
Dismiss the charge for want of prosecution
testPool.explanation: No indication is treated as an indicated not guilty plea for these purposes, so the case proceeds to the allocation procedure exactly as on an express not guilty indication.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common error in this lesson is assuming offence seriousness determines the first court of appearance, or that a not guilty plea sends a case straight to the Crown Court. Neither is right — every case starts in the magistrates' court, and only the allocation procedure (next lesson) actually decides venue for a contested either-way case.
